11	regions outside ordinary globular classes.

14	- `fold`: similar major secondary structures in the same arrangement and
15	  topology.
16	- `superfamily`: families inferred to share common evolutionary origin from
17	  structural, functional, and sequence evidence.
18	- `family`: a closer relationship, usually supported by sequence similarity or
19	  very similar function and structure.
20	- `protein`: essentially the same function across species or isoforms.
21	- `species`: a distinct sequence and its variants in SCOPe terminology.
22	- `domain`: a classified structural instance with a SID and SUNID.
23	
24	Family and superfamily are homology-bearing levels. Fold and class alone are
25	structural categories, not positive SCOPe assertions of common ancestry.
26	
27	## Relationship Decisions
28	
29	For two domains:
30	
31	1. Retrieve both lineages in the same release.
32	2. Identify the deepest shared class, fold, superfamily, and family nodes.
33	3. Check annotations and homology warnings for both domains.
34	4. State only the relationship justified by the evidence:
35	   - shared family: close SCOPe relationship;
36	   - shared superfamily but different families: probable common ancestry;
37	   - shared fold but different superfamilies: structural/topological
38	     similarity, not a SCOPe homology assertion;
39	   - shared class only: broad architectural similarity.
40	
41	Do not infer a specific reaction, substrate, ligand, pathway role, phenotype,
42	oligomeric state, or interchangeable template from a superfamily assignment.
43	Those conclusions require additional sequence, active-site, ligand,
44	domain-architecture, genomic-context, or experimental evidence.
45	
46	Different superfamilies are also not a positive SCOPe assertion of analogy,
47	convergence, independent origin, or absence of homology. Use the asymmetric
48	statement: SCOPe supports shared fold-level structure but does not assert
49	superfamily-level common ancestry. A stronger positive or negative
50	evolutionary conclusion needs independent evidence.
51	
52	When explaining a proposed remote relationship, distinguish evidence that was
53	actually inspected from evidence that would be needed. Relevant evidence can
54	include a global structural alignment and matching topology, sequence
55	correspondence at equivalent core positions, conserved motifs in equivalent
56	structural contexts, compatible domain architecture and biological context,
57	phylogenetic support, and experiments. Do not list these as observations
58	unless the source or result was retrieved.
59	
60	## Domain Boundaries And Modularity
61	
62	A domain need not be contiguous in sequence. Insertions and rearrangements can
63	place one evolutionary module inside another. Compare domains rather than whole
64	chains so unrelated inserts, tags, or adjacent domains do not create false
65	similarity or obscure a real relationship.
66	
67	Historical boundary changes can reflect newly observed evolutionary contexts.
68	Do not describe a particular change unless every compared release was queried.
69	
70	## Special Annotations
71	
72	Machine-readable heterogeneity annotations can qualify ordinary hierarchy
73	interpretation:
74	
75	- `md`: multiple alternative domain divisions.
76	- `re`: repeat-based domains with different repeat counts.
77	- `fr`: fragment.
78	- `as`: additional subdomains.
79	- `ie`: additional insertions or extensions.
80	- `ms`: missing secondary structures.
81	- `ae`: additional elements.
82	- `me`: missing elements.
83	- `nf`: not a true fold.
84	- `hf`: heterogeneous fold.
85	- `dn`: different domains contain different subsets of subdomains.
86	
87	Artifacts, synthetic tags, fragments, repeats, heterogeneous families, and
88	"not true" groupings should not be used as ordinary homology or benchmark
89	examples without preserving the caveat.
90	
91	Annotations constrain an interpretation; they do not automatically erase a
92	family or superfamily relationship. Explain exactly which inference is
93	affected.
94	
95	## Representative Selection
96	
97	ASTRAL subsets reduce sequence redundancy. SPACI and AEROSPACI support
98	technical-quality comparisons and representative selection. They are not
99	evolutionary or functional scores.
100	
101	Retrieve quality records for every candidate. Compare actual values together
102	with method, resolution, R factor, and available validation fields. A
103	technically preferred representative does not replace alternative ligand,
104	conformational, oligomeric, or biological states.
105	
106	Never rank candidates when the requested quality measure is unavailable for
107	one or more of them.
108	
109	## Dataset Design
110	
111	For remote-homology benchmarks:
112	
113	- Separate training and test examples by family while keeping positives within
114	  a verified superfamily.
115	- Use same-fold, different-superfamily examples only as labeled operational
116	  `SCOPe-negative` pairs, meaning no SCOPe superfamily-level homology assertion.
117	  They are not proven biological nonhomologs. Preserve annotations and run
118	  sensitivity analyses because future evidence or curation can reveal remote
119	  relationships.
120	- Remove sequence leakage with an appropriate ASTRAL nonredundant subset.
121	- Preserve biologically meaningful diversity rather than selecting only the
122	  single highest-quality structure.
123	- Exclude or stratify artifacts, fragments, repeats, and heterogeneous
124	  groupings.
125	- Freeze the SCOPe release, selection rules, thresholds, and representative
126	  choices.
127	
128	## Automated Classification
129	
130	SCOPe combines manual curation with validated automated classification.
131	Automation is useful for placing new structures into established regions of
132	the hierarchy. Manual curation remains important for new folds and
133	superfamilies, remote relationships, artifacts, boundary corrections,
134	heterogeneity, and large complexes.
135	
136	Do not equate automated classification with low quality. Report automated
137	status when it affects provenance or interpretation.
138	
139	## Epistemic Boundaries
140	
141	Separate four kinds of statement:
142	
143	1. **Retrieved fact:** directly present in a cited API response.
144	2. **SCOPe interpretation:** follows from the retrieved hierarchy and
145	   annotation semantics.
146	3. **Biological hypothesis:** plausible but requires evidence outside SCOPe.
147	4. **Unknown from available data:** cannot be determined because a necessary
148	   record was not retrieved or the API does not expose it.
149	
150	Use qualified language for hypotheses. Use explicit abstention for unknown
151	release-specific facts. Do not convert uncertainty into a confident database
152	claim. In particular, a retrieved classification change does not by itself
153	retrieve the structural, sequence, or functional rationale for that change.

VERIFIED RELEASE FACTS

SCOP 1.75: PDB 1acc chain A carried exactly one domain, d1acca_ (SUNID 43828), SCCS f.11.1.1, description "1acc A:" covering the whole chain. Its lineage was class f (Membrane and cell surface proteins and peptides), fold f.11 (Anthrax protective antigen, SUNID 56987), superfamily f.11.1 (SUNID 56988), family f.11.1.1 (SUNID 56989), protein node 56990, species Bacillus anthracis TaxId 1392 (SUNID 56991). Annotation comment: "complexed with ca". No heterogeneity entries or homology warnings were returned.

SCOPe 2.08 (stable, freeze 2021-07-28, release 2021-09-22): the same chain is split into two domains with new SIDs and new lineages.

- d1acca2, SUNID 238522, SCCS b.179.1.1, residues A:14-225. Class b (All beta proteins, SUNID 48724), fold b.179 (Anthrax protective antigen N-terminal-like, SUNID 254104), superfamily b.179.1 (PA14-like, SUNID 254123), family b.179.1.1 (PA14, SUNID 254147).
- d1acca1, SUNID 238521, SCCS f.60.1.1, residues A:226-735. Class f, fold f.60 (Anthrax protective antigen C-terminal-like, SUNID 254103), superfamily f.60.1 (SUNID 254122), family f.60.1.1 (SUNID 254146).

The old fold node SUNID 56987 (f.11) is not found in release 2.08, consistent with retirement of the single whole-chain classification rather than its retention alongside the split. Both 2.08 domains keep the "complexed with ca" comment and return no heterogeneity annotation such as md, fr, re, or ie, and no domain-level homology warnings.

WHAT THE NEW NODES CONTAIN

The PA14-like superfamily b.179.1 in 2.08 now holds four families: PA14 (b.179.1.1), GLEYA domain (b.179.1.2), Glycoside hydrolase family 31 (GH31) PA14-like domain (b.179.1.3), and automated matches (b.179.1.0). The PA14 family itself contains two protein nodes, PA14 (SUNID 254334, which holds the 1acc domain) and Beta-glucosidase PA14 domain (SUNID 254417). By contrast, superfamily f.60.1 has a single family, f.60.1.1. The f.60 fold node carries a curator comment stating that this region is the C-terminal three domains: II (226-487) beta-sandwiches of gamma-crystallin-like topology similar to domain I, III (488-594) with a beta-grasp-like fold, and IV (595-735) with an Ig-like fold. The f.60 homology section explicitly returns homology_implied_by_level false with the note that levels above superfamily do not imply homology.

BIOLOGICAL MEANING FOR DOMAINS AS EVOLUTIONARY MODULES

The change converts a protein-specific, one-structure classification into a modular one. In 1.75 the whole chain was its own fold, superfamily, family, protein, and species lineage: a taxonomically isolated entry whose hierarchy asserted nothing about any other protein. In 2.08 the N-terminal segment A:14-225 is placed in a superfamily shared with carbohydrate-binding modules found in fungal adhesins (GLEYA), glycoside hydrolase family 31 enzymes, and beta-glucosidase, while the C-terminal A:226-735 segment keeps a toxin-specific lineage in class f.

This is the modular point. The excised N-terminal module is the evolutionary unit that recurs across proteins with entirely different overall architectures and biological roles, whereas the chain as a whole recurs nowhere. A domain boundary is therefore a hypothesis about the recombining unit of evolution, and it is revisable: as homologues of one segment were observed in other contexts, the curated unit shrank to match the segment that is actually shared. The 1.75 boundary was not wrong given what was then classified; it was less informative because no partial homologue had yet forced the split. The f.60 curator comment also shows that the remaining C-terminal classification is itself an aggregate of three structurally distinguishable sub-regions (II, III, IV) with gamma-crystallin-like, beta-grasp-like, and Ig-like folds, so that part of the chain is a candidate for further subdivision rather than a settled single module. I did not retrieve any record asserting that those sub-regions are separate SCOPe domains in 2.08, and the retrieved 2.08 chain record lists exactly two domains.

CONSEQUENCES FOR HOMOLOGY SEARCHING

1. Search and score per domain, not per chain. A whole-chain 1acc query mixes a PA14-like beta module with an unrelated toxin-specific region. That dilutes alignment statistics for true PA14 relatives and can generate alignments that straddle a boundary where no shared ancestry is claimed. Use d1acca2 (A:14-225) and d1acca1 (A:226-735) as separate queries.

2. Expect and respect partial coverage. A genuine remote relative of 1acc may align over only about a quarter of the chain. Coverage filters requiring most of the query length would discard the correct PA14-like hits. Conversely, a hit confined to A:14-225 says nothing about A:226-735.

3. Direct homology claims to the right level. A hit landing in family b.179.1.1 (PA14) is a close SCOPe relationship. A hit in a sibling family such as GLEYA or the GH31 PA14-like family shares superfamily b.179.1, which supports probable common ancestry but not shared biochemistry. Shared fold b.179 or f.60, or shared class alone, is structural similarity only; the f.60 homology record states directly that levels above superfamily do not imply homology.

4. Do not transfer function across the split. Superfamily co-membership of d1acca2 with glycoside hydrolase and adhesin PA14 modules does not make the anthrax module a carbohydrate-active enzyme component, and it does not make the fungal or GH31 proteins toxin components. Likewise, membrane and cell-surface class placement of d1acca1 is not evidence of receptor binding, pore formation, calcium dependence, or any specific ligand for any relative. The only ligand evidence retrieved is the comment "complexed with ca" on 1acc itself, which is a crystallographic annotation for this entry, not a family property.

5. Freeze the release and remap identifiers. Any pipeline, benchmark, or dataset built on d1acca_ or on SCCS f.11.1.1 is tied to 1.75 and will not resolve the same way in 2.08: the SID, the SUNIDs, the SCCS codes, the fold, and even the class of part of the chain all changed, and the old f.11 fold node returns not_found in 2.08. Old f.11-labelled training or test examples must be relabelled, and any same-fold or different-fold pair list regenerated, or the labels will be internally inconsistent. State the release explicitly in reproducible work.

6. Treat the split as a caution about negatives. The 1.75 state would have supported a claim that this chain had no classified relatives. That claim would now be wrong for its N-terminal module. Absence of a SCOPe relationship in any one release is not evidence of absence of homology, and future curation can split a domain again, in particular for the three sub-regions described in the f.60 comment.

7. Template use. Neither d1acca1 nor d1acca2 should be used as a modelling or threading template for a target matched over only the other segment. Template transfer requires the aligned region to correspond to the domain actually matched, with a verified residue mapping; the residue ranges above are PDB author numbering as given in the SCOPe descriptions.

LIMITS

I verified that the classification changed, with the full before and after lineages, by querying releases 1.75 and 2.08 separately. I did not retrieve the sequence, structural, or literature rationale that drove the split, nor the intermediate release in which it first occurred; the annotation and homology sections returned no inconsistency or heterogeneity flags that would explain it, and the f.60 comment describes current sub-structure rather than the curation decision. No BLAST or FATCAT evidence was retrieved here, so no non-official regional relationship is proposed. Membership of other families in superfamily b.179.1 is a retrieved SCOPe assertion of probable common ancestry at that level; I did not retrieve the individual domain lineages of those other families, so no pairwise relationship between 1acc and a specific other structure is asserted.
